Kiribati moved the International Date Line so the whole country could share one date.
Before 1995 its islands sat on both sides of the line, a whole day apart. After the change, its eastern islands were among the first places to see the year 2000.
Lake Baikal in Russia holds about a fifth of all the fresh water on Earth's surface.
It is also the deepest lake, more than 1,600 metres, and about 25 million years old.
The place on Earth farthest from any land is called Point Nemo.
It is in the South Pacific, about 2,700 km from the nearest island. Often the closest people are astronauts on the space station passing overhead.
France has more time zones than any other country.
Thanks to islands and territories around the world, from the Caribbean to the Pacific, it spans 12 time zones, or 13 with its Antarctic claim.
China uses one clock time across land that is about five time zones wide.
In the far west, in Xinjiang, the sun can rise at around 10 in the morning on the official clock.
Nepal's clocks are set 5 hours and 45 minutes ahead of world time.
It is one of only a few places in the world whose time is offset by 45 minutes.
Nepal's flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
It is two stacked triangles, said to stand for the Himalayas and for two religions.
Sudan has more ancient pyramids than Egypt.
More than 200 pyramids stand in old Nubian sites like Meroë. They are smaller and steeper than Egypt's.
Ethiopia has its own calendar, with 13 months.
Twelve months have 30 days and a short 13th month has five or six. The Ethiopian year is about seven to eight years behind the one used in most countries.
Japan counted its islands again in 2023 and found it has more than 14,000.
Better digital maps showed 14,125 islands, more than double the old number of 6,852. The land did not change, the counting did.
Lesotho is the only country where every bit of land is more than 1,000 metres above the sea.
Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres high, the highest lowest point of any country.
Tristan da Cunha is one of the most remote places people live.
Fewer than 300 people live there, about 2,400 km from the nearest neighbours on Saint Helena. There is no airport, only boats.
Monaco is smaller than New York's Central Park.
The whole country covers about 2 square kilometres. Central Park is about 3.4.
No bridge crosses the Amazon River anywhere along its main length.
The river runs through rainforest with few roads, and its banks flood and move, so ferries do the job.
Saudi Arabia does not have a single permanent river.
It has dry valleys called wadis that fill only after rain. Much of its drinking water comes from taking salt out of seawater.
Russia and the USA are only about 4 km apart at one spot.
Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (USA) islands sit on either side of the International Date Line, so they are almost a day apart in time.
Finland has around three million saunas for about 5.6 million people.
That is roughly one for every two people. UNESCO listed Finnish sauna culture as world heritage in 2020.
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level.
Dykes, dunes and pumps keep the sea and rivers out. The country's lowest point is about 7 metres below sea level.
The world's tallest waterfall is named after a pilot.
Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979 metres. American pilot Jimmie Angel landed his plane on top of the mountain in 1937.
The Great Wall of China is not visible from space with your eyes alone.
It is long but narrow, about the colour of the land around it. Astronauts have said they could not pick it out.
The Eiffel Tower grows about 15 cm taller in summer.
Iron expands when it heats up, so on hot days the tower stretches upwards a little.
The name 'Silk Road' was invented in 1877, long after the trade routes were used.
German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coined it. It was really a web of many routes carrying silk, spices, paper and ideas.
Papua New Guinea has about 840 living languages, more than any other country.
Mountains and thick forest kept groups apart for thousands of years, so languages grew separately.
Bhutan only allowed television in 1999.
It was one of the last countries in the world to switch TV on, and the internet arrived the same year.
A gas crater in Turkmenistan has been on fire since around 1971.
Called the Darvaza crater, or 'Door to Hell', it is believed to have been set alight on purpose to burn off dangerous gas.
Many of the giant stone heads on Easter Island have bodies buried underground.
Digs showed some of the moai have full torsos hidden under soil that built up over the centuries.
Angkor Wat in Cambodia is the largest religious monument on Earth.
It was built in the 1100s, first as a Hindu temple and later used as a Buddhist one. It even appears on Cambodia's flag.
Borobudur in Indonesia is the largest Buddhist temple in the world.
Built in the 800s on Java, it has more than 500 Buddha statues and was hidden under volcanic ash and jungle for centuries.
In 2021, one stuck ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days.
The Ever Given, about 400 metres long, wedged sideways. Hundreds of ships queued at both ends.
A ship crossing the Panama Canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific ends up further east.
The canal runs from north-west to south-east because of how the land curves, so the Pacific end is east of the Atlantic end.
The USA bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars.
That worked out to about 2 US cents for each acre of land.
Only two countries are 'doubly landlocked': Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan.
That means they have no coast, and every country around them has no coast either.
The Sahara Desert was green with lakes about 6,000 to 11,000 years ago.
Rock art there shows giraffes, hippos and cattle. Small changes in Earth's wobble shifted the rains away.
The point on Earth closest to the stars is not the top of Everest.
It is the top of Chimborazo in Ecuador. Earth bulges at the equator, so that peak sits furthest from Earth's centre.
Measured from its base on the sea floor, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller than Everest.
It rises more than 10,000 metres from the bottom of the Pacific, but most of it is under water.
Norway keeps more than a million seed samples inside a frozen mountain.
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores spare seeds of crops from almost every country, as a backup for the world's food.
Singapore has grown by about a quarter since the 1960s, by building land into the sea.
It used sand and soil to reclaim land, which is why its map keeps changing.
The Maldives is the flattest country in the world.
Its land is on average only about 1.5 metres above the sea, which makes rising seas a serious worry.
Nauru has no official capital city.
It is one of the smallest countries, about 21 square kilometres. Government offices are in a district called Yaren.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world.
It has well over 100 letters in English. Thai people simply call the city Krung Thep, City of Angels.
Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia is the coldest capital city in the world.
Its average yearly temperature is below freezing, and winter nights can fall below minus 40 °C.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
Counting all its islands, it stretches more than 200,000 kilometres, enough to wrap around Earth about five times.
Australia is wider than the Moon.
Australia is about 4,000 km from east to west. The Moon is about 3,500 km across.
Venice is built on millions of wooden posts pushed into mud.
Without air, the wood under water hardly rots, so many posts have held the city up for centuries.
Liechtenstein once rented out the whole country.
In 2011 a company offered it for events, with custom street signs and even a special money of your own, for about 70,000 dollars a night.
The Dead Sea is shrinking by about a metre a year.
Rivers that fed it are used for farms and towns, and mineral companies take water from it too.
Mount Everest grows a few millimetres every year.
India's land is still pushing into Asia, slowly lifting the Himalayas.
Greenland is about 80 percent covered in ice.
If all its ice melted, seas around the world would rise by about 7 metres.
The Atacama Desert in Chile has places where rain has hardly ever been recorded.
It is so dry that NASA tests Mars rovers there.
Iceland grows bananas.
Greenhouses heated by hot water from volcanoes have grown bananas there since the 1940s.
The Caspian Sea is really the world's biggest lake.
It is surrounded by land on all sides, but its water is slightly salty, so it was named a sea.
Africa is slowly splitting in two.
Along the East African Rift, the land pulls apart by a few millimetres a year. In millions of years, a new ocean may form.
Spain's Canary Islands have a whistled language.
Silbo Gomero turns Spanish into whistles that carry across deep valleys on La Gomera. Children learn it at school.
Mexico City is sinking.
Parts of it drop up to about 50 cm a year because water is pumped from under the old lake bed it is built on.
A town in Norway called Longyearbyen tells people not to die there.
Bodies do not rot in its frozen ground, so very ill people are flown to the mainland.
The flag of Mozambique has an AK-47 rifle on it.
It is crossed with a hoe and a book, standing for defence, farming and education.
In Japan there are vending machines selling hot meals, umbrellas and even fresh eggs.
Japan has about one vending machine for every 30 people.
Some 40 percent of people on Earth live within about 100 km of the sea.
Coasts are good for trade and fishing, which is why so many big cities grew there.
Esperanto, a language invented on purpose, has native speakers.
L. L. Zamenhof created it in 1887 to help people talk across borders. Some families raise children speaking it from birth.
The Andes are the longest mountain range above water.
They run about 7,000 km along the west side of South America, through seven countries.
